entities.name: Louis Marie Florent du Châtelet
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Louis-Marie-Florent de Lomont d'Haraucourt, duc du Châtelet, embodied the twilight of the Ancien Régime's aristocratic military and diplomatic elite, serving as a prominent French general and ambassador during the decades preceding the French Revolution. Born into one of France's most ancient noble families on November 20, 1727, in Semur-en-Auxois, he inherited the ducal title in 1786. His career spanned significant European conflicts like the Seven Years' War and critical diplomatic postings to the Court of St. James's, placing him at the nexus of Anglo-French relations during a period of intense imperial rivalry and shifting alliances. His actions and eventual fate during the Revolution highlight the profound societal upheaval that dismantled the very system he represented.

Du Châtelet's military service began early, seeing him rise through the ranks to Lieutenant General in 1780. He commanded the Régiment de Navarre and later the Gardes Françaises, a pivotal unit in the defense of Paris. His diplomatic career included a crucial ambassadorship to Great Britain from 1767 to 1770, where he navigated the complex aftermath of the Seven Years' War and attempted to stabilize relations between the two great powers. His administrative roles, such as governor of Picardy, further cemented his position within the Bourbon monarchy's highest echelons.

The duc du Châtelet's legacy is irrevocably tied to the collapse of the world he served. Despite his initial reformist sympathies and efforts to maintain order, his aristocratic status and loyalty to the monarchy made him a target of the radical Jacobin government during the Reign of Terror. Arrested in 1793, he was condemned by the Revolutionary Tribunal and executed by guillotine, becoming one of the many noble victims whose deaths symbolized the complete rupture with the feudal past.

His specific role as ambassador to Great Britain and commander of the Gardes Françaises underscore his direct involvement in crucial pre-revolutionary events.
